To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the incorporation of purified, calf thymus, double stranded DNA into hamster embryo cell culture, followed by exposure of the cells to carcinogenic and/or noncarcinogenic chemical agents resulted in permanent cell line conversion; and (2) the converted cells did not induce tumors in compatible animals inoculation.
the incorporation of inactive DNA into cultured mammalian cells renders them susceptible to conversion to permanent cell lines by carcinogenic and non-carcinogenic chemical agents.
the presence of DNA in cells can enhance the effects of chemical mutagens and carcinogens, and that this synergistic effect is analogous to the effects of DNA viruses on the buccal mucosa.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synergistic effect of mutagenic agents and incorporated DNA in the induction of malignant transformation in cultured cells.
the possible synergistic effect of mutagenic agents and DNA in carcinogenesis.
the effects of carcinogenic chemicals and viruses in the buccal cavity, which is the most frequent site of origin of human squamous cell carcinomas.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
carcinogenesis is not a simple process but is the result of multiple factors.
the incorporation of DNA into cultured hamster cells and subsequent exposure to carcinogenic and nongenotoxic agents resulted in conversion to permanent cell lines.
DNA incorporation into cells in vitro is an excellent experimental system to study the synergistic effect of carcinogenic chemicals and incorporated DNA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the DNA virus and the environmental mutagen are both necessary for malignant transformation of the host cell.
DNA viruses and environmental mutagens, when acting synergistically, might be the etiologic agents for oral and oropharyngeal cancers.
the incorporation of inactive, exogenous DNA may be a cofactor in carcinogenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the buccal cavity is a potential site of carcinogenesis.
we have developed a new method of studying the synergistic effect of mutagenic chemicals with incorporated DNA on cultured hamster embryo (CHE) cells.
DNA is not a carcinogen but may act to potentiate the carcinogenicity of other environmental agents.
